name: Lena Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on my aunt and uncle's farm, Brookside, which has a bit of everything: sixty ewes, twenty beef cattle, potatoes, a few fields of barley, and the farm shop by the road. Mornings I'm with Uncle Rob doing the stock, feeding, checking, moving sheep. From eleven I'm usually in the shop with Aunt Jen, serving, restocking the meat counter and bagging potatoes, and Saturdays it's shop all day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the shop, if I'm honest, more than the field. You get Mrs Patel who comes every Tuesday for two chops and tells me about her grandson, and the walkers who want a sausage roll and directions. What wears me out is lambing in March, because I'm still not good at it, and Rob's patience runs thin when he's had no sleep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up at Brookside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was doing admin at a car dealership after school and hated being inside. Rob's knees started going two years ago, and Jen asked if I'd come and help. Family helps family, that's how we were raised. I live with my partner Matt, he's an electrician, in the village, so it's a five-minute walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy and leave it at that. I'd maybe post the shop's opening hours with a nicer picture, if the AI helped. Most of our customers wouldn't notice anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I might get the shop's posts done quicker. I use one of those AI apps sometimes to write the Facebook post about what's in this week, because Jen wants one every Friday. That's about as far as it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. I'd keep learning the stock side from Rob, and maybe do the butchery course so I can help on the meat counter properly. Matt and I have about four months saved and we'd keep adding to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing changes that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the Friday post usually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New potatoes in, lamb from our own fields, Jen's lemon cake is back. The AI wanted to call it artisan, and Jen made me take that out. She said we're a farm shop, not a hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the shop that worries you, even now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big supermarket on the ring road, mostly. They opened a local food section with farm photos on it, and the prices are lower than ours. But they don't know Mrs Patel's grandson's name, and that's what keeps people coming.

S0.say: I'd say it's handy and leave it at that, maybe posting the shop's hours with a nicer picture. Most of our customers wouldn't notice a thing.
S0.think: I might get the shop's Friday Facebook post done quicker, because I already use an AI app for it sometimes. That's about as far as it goes for me.
S0.do: Keeps learning stock work from her uncle and looks at a butchery course for the meat counter. Adds to the four months of savings she shares with Matt.
S0.feel: Calm, because nothing that matters changes.
S0.quote: The AI wanted to call it artisan, and Jen made me take that out. She said we're a farm shop, not a hotel.
S0.fieldNote: Lena lights up about the shop and its regulars far more than the fieldwork. She uses AI lightly and her aunt edits it. The supermarket, not AI, is the competitor on her mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is the right way, give people time. If companies hire fewer beginners, that's sad, but family businesses will always need young people. I'd say get an apprenticeship or work for family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm lucky. I've got a job because I'm family, not because I'm good at lambing. If Brookside wasn't my aunt's, I'm not sure anyone would have hired me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brookside and get properly good at things, the butchery, the lambing. I'd maybe ask my cousin Ellie, who's sixteen, to do Saturdays in the shop so she gets a start too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's honest, saying you got the job through family. Does it bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, sometimes, when Rob redoes something I did. But that's what family farms are, you learn on the job and someone patient covers for you. I'd do the same for Ellie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be training young people, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Businesses and families first, with apprenticeships, and the government can help with the cost. I don't think colleges alone teach you a farm. You learn sheep by standing in the pen in the rain.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is the right way and family businesses will always need young people. Young people should get an apprenticeship or work for family.
S1.think: I'm lucky, because I've got this job through family, not because I'm good at lambing. If Brookside wasn't my aunt's, I'm not sure anyone would have hired me.
S1.do: Stays at Brookside to get properly good at butchery and lambing. Asks her sixteen-year-old cousin Ellie to work Saturdays in the shop so she gets a start.
S1.quote: You learn sheep by standing in the pen in the rain.
S1.fieldNote: Her honesty about getting the job through family was striking. Her traditional views show in trusting families and businesses to train people, with government only helping with cost. She'd pass the favour on to her cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard on office people and they should look at trades and farms, there's work if you want it. Matt can't find enough apprentices as it is. I'd say government should help with retraining, but people have to want to work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the shop is what I'd think about. A lot of our weekend customers are office people from town who like a drive and a nice lunch. If they're worried about money, they go to the supermarket instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Jen about cheaper things, like a sausage bap deal, value packs of mince, potatoes by the sack. I'd post more on Facebook about prices being fair, not just nice. And I'd hold off on the butchery course until we know the shop's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The shop's the heart of the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the shop had a bad year, what would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my Saturday hours, honestly, Jen would do it herself to save the wage. Then the cakes, because they take her all Thursday night. I'd hate that, the cakes are half the reason people stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people have to want to work. Is that fair to office workers who lose jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it sounded harder than I meant. Most of them would want to work, I'm sure. I'm just saying the work out here exists, and someone has to tell them it's there.

S2.say: I'd say office workers should look at trades and farms, because there's work if you want it. Government should help with retraining, but people have to want to work too.
S2.think: I'd really think about the shop, because many weekend customers are office workers from town. If they're worried about money, they'll go to the supermarket instead.
S2.do: Suggests cheaper lines to Jen, like sausage bap deals, value mince and sacks of potatoes, and posts about fair prices. Puts off the butchery course until the shop looks safe.
S2.feel: Uneasy, because the shop is the heart of the place.
S2.quote: I'd hate that, the cakes are half the reason people stop.
S2.fieldNote: Her public line was a bit hard on office workers, and she softened it when I asked. Her real worry is the shop's weekend trade. She'd lose her own Saturday hours before the shop lost anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people shouldn't be punished for doing well, but the ones doing well should look after their own towns, spend locally, give to the village. I'd want it sorted by communities, not by politicians shouting. I wouldn't march about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this might be okay for Brookside. People with booming shares buy expensive lamb and lemon cake. But house prices booming means Matt and I won't buy in the village, and that's where my whole family is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Jen to sell more meat boxes to the well-off people in the new houses by the golf course. I'd ask Rob whether there's any chance we could build or convert a little place on the farm one day. And we'd keep saving, every month, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Shop's fine, but the village could change around us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Change how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Second homes, people from the city who come at weekends and complain about the smell of muck. It's already started, three houses on Church Lane. They buy the cakes but they don't come to the harvest supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would want the government to share out the gains. Where do you stand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some help, yes, for people who lose jobs and can't find another. But I'd rather it went through local things, the school, the village hall, apprenticeships, than cheques in the post. People need something to get up for.

S3.say: I'd say people shouldn't be punished for doing well, but they should look after their own towns and spend locally. I'd want communities to sort it, not politicians shouting.
S3.think: This might be fine for Brookside, since people with booming shares buy expensive lamb and cake. But house prices mean Matt and I won't buy in the village where my family is.
S3.do: Pushes meat boxes to the well-off buyers in the new houses by the golf course. Asks her uncle about building or converting a small home on the farm and keeps saving monthly.
S3.feel: Uneasy, because the shop is fine but the village could change around them.
S3.quote: They buy the cakes but they don't come to the harvest supper.
S3.fieldNote: She sees the boom as good for trade and bad for the village. Second homes on Church Lane are already a sore point. She'd rather support go through local schools and halls than cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms might help with the heavy work, Rob's knees would thank them. But I'd say a farm shop needs a person at the counter, and people will pay for that. I'd say slow it down so families can adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the stock side worries me. If Rob buys a robot that feeds and checks the cattle, then the mornings I do are gone, and I'm not good enough at lambing to be worth keeping for that. The shop would be my job then, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the neighbours buy and whether it works, I wouldn't rush. I'd move more of my hours into the shop and finally do the butchery course, because robots won't be cutting chops at Brookside any time soon. I'd also ask Matt to learn about fitting and fixing the robots, because someone will need to wire them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the shop, for the farm side, and for Rob, who'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Rob hate it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he's done it by hand for forty years, and his dad before him. He'd buy the robot to save his knees and then stand in the yard watching it, muttering. I can already hear him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could robots come to the shop too, the till and the meat counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The till, maybe, the big shops already have self-checkouts. But people come to us to talk to someone. If Mrs Patel had to talk to a screen about her grandson, she'd stop coming, and I wouldn't blame her.

S4.say: I'd say robots might help with heavy farm work, and Rob's knees would thank them. But a farm shop needs a person at the counter, so slow it down so families can adjust.
S4.think: The stock side worries me, because a feeding robot would take my mornings. I'm not good enough at lambing to be kept for that, so the shop would become my whole job.
S4.do: Waits to see what neighbouring farms buy before acting, and moves more of her hours into the shop. Finally takes the butchery course and asks Matt to learn how to fit and fix farm robots.
S4.feel: Anxious, mostly for the farm side and for her uncle, who'd hate it.
S4.quote: He'd buy the robot to save his knees and then stand in the yard watching it, muttering.
S4.fieldNote: Her steady side shows: wait for the neighbours, then move. She has a clear fallback in the shop and believes people pay for a person. Her uncle's pride came through more than her own fear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because it's the only one that really reaches the farm. What would help is support for small family farms to buy the kit together, and apprenticeships, so young people still learn the real work. And keep the village affordable for the people who grew up there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the farm shops. They're where farms meet towns, and if the towns get poorer or the villages get empty, we feel it first. Jen says the shop is the farm's front door, and she's right.

headlineQuote: If Mrs Patel had to talk to a screen about her grandson, she'd stop coming, and I wouldn't blame her.
portrait: Lena is a 27-year-old working on her aunt and uncle's mixed farm, splitting her days between the livestock and the farm shop she loves. She's frank that she got the job through family and isn't yet good at lambing, and she believes in family, apprenticeships and local community over government. In the middle pictures she worries mainly about the shop's customers tightening their belts and about second homes changing the village. In the robot picture she expects to lose her stock work and would move fully into the shop and learn butchery, sure that customers come for a person at the counter.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots picture, because a feeding robot would take her morning stock work and she isn't skilled enough at lambing to be kept for that.
whatWouldHelp: Support for small family farms to buy new equipment together, apprenticeships for young people, and keeping the village affordable for local families.
